Debt Lab

The Reef's fishing code is four years old. A new lure takes 10 developer-days and often breaks something. Choose how to deal with it (keep patching, rewrite it all, or replace it piece by piece), whether to write tests first, and how much time goes to debt, then watch 26 weeks of a 4-person team.

Half a year, 4 developers. Goal by week 26: a new lure costs at most 5 days, at least 60 lures and features shipped, and at most 25 bugs reach players.

Lesson 065: technical debt

    What this shows

    Debt is interest, paid on every feature

    Every lure on tangled code costs more and makes the next one cost more. Patching ships steadily slower.

    Big rewrites ship nothing for a long time

    The old code holds years of hidden behaviour. Finding it again doubles the estimate, and the live game still needs the old code meanwhile.

    Replace piece by piece, with tests

    Pin today's behaviour with tests, put an interface in front of one part, replace it, repeat. Features keep shipping, and each finished part makes them cheaper.

    This lab is a model, not a measurement. It uses Lesson 065's numbers: 4 developers, 20 developer-days a week. A lure costs 4 × (1 + 1.5 × debt) days; debt starts at 1.0 (10 days a lure) and patching adds 0.03 per lure. Each bug-prone change sends 0.5 × (1 + debt) bugs to players, 60% fewer with tests. Replacing one of 5 parts costs 16 days (20 with tests first) and cuts debt by 0.18; a part replaced without tests loses 3 behaviours players notice. The rewrite was estimated at 120 days but takes 240 (+20 for tests), with 30% of the team kept on the live game; without tests it ships with 15 lost behaviours.
